subsection: 7. Case study: the Oil Crisis, 1973, and the Western economies, 1973–1990; Margaret Thatcher

notes.b: The oil crisis struck economies that had grown fast for almost thirty years after the Second World War. To see why the shock hurt so much, you need to know what governments and markets had been doing before it.
points: From 1945 to 1973 Western Europe enjoyed a boom of rapid growth and full employment (almost everyone who wanted a job had one), helped by Marshall Aid (American money for reconstruction) and free trade. The earlier notes on the Western economies cover this in detail.

Governments followed Keynesian economics, which means managing demand (spending in the economy) through taxes and public spending to keep employment high. In Britain the main parties accepted this as the post-war consensus, so it was seen as normal, not controversial.
The welfare state is state provision of health care, pensions, benefits and education, paid for out of taxes. It was affordable in the boom, but unemployment and rising costs after 1973 strained it.

Capitalism is an economic system of private ownership, competitive markets and profit. Western economies stayed capitalist in the boom, but with heavy state management; Thatcher's aim later was to extend market freedom through privatisation and free markets.
notes.tip: Essays that combine boom and recession reward you for linking the two halves: present the oil crisis as the end of the boom, not as a separate story.

notes.h: Background and causes: oil dependence and the Arab-Israeli conflict
notes.b: By 1973 Western Europe relied on cheap imported oil, and the Arab oil producers had both grievances and organisations through which to act. The economy was also already becoming unstable before the shock.
points: Oil had become Western Europe's main energy source during the 1950s and 1960s, supplying about half or more of its energy by 1973. Most of it was imported from the Middle East and bought in dollars.
The price had stayed low, at about three dollars a barrel before October 1973, so cheap energy fuelled the boom. This is why any sudden rise in price (an oil shock) was bound to hit importers hard.

OPEC (the Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries) was formed in 1960 by oil producers generally. OAPEC (the Organisation of Arab Petroleum Exporting Countries) was formed in 1968 and had only Arab members, who had long sought higher prices.
Israel was created in 1948. In the Six-Day War of June 1967 it occupied Sinai, Gaza, the West Bank, East Jerusalem and the Golan Heights, which became a lasting grievance of the Arab producers.

Inflation (a general rise in prices) had been rising since the late 1960s. Bretton Woods, the system of fixed exchange rates, ended in 1971-73 when the USA ended dollar convertibility to gold in August 1971, so the boom was already weakening.
notes.tip: Do not mix up OPEC (1960, all producers) and OAPEC (1968, Arab members only): the October 1973 price rise came from the Gulf members of OPEC, while the output cuts and embargo came from OAPEC.

notes.h: The Yom Kippur War and the price rise, October 1973
notes.b: A new Arab-Israeli war gave the Arab producers their opportunity. They answered it with a price rise and cuts in output, using oil as a weapon for the first time.
points: The Yom Kippur War began on 6 October 1973 when Egypt and Syria attacked Israel. The USA resupplied Israel with arms during the war, which led the Arab states to use oil as a weapon against Israel's supporters.
On 16 October 1973 OPEC's Gulf members raised the posted price (the official price at which they sold oil) by about 70 per cent.
On 17 October OAPEC announced output cuts of 5 per cent a month until Israel withdrew from the occupied territories, so less oil reached the market while prices climbed.
The war ended in a ceasefire in late October, following UN Security Council Resolution 338 of 22 October. Western governments then reassessed how dependent they were on imported energy.
notes.tip: Ordinary Level answers earn one mark for each correct dated statement, so learn 6 October (war begins), 16 October (price rise) and 17 October (output cuts).

notes.h: The embargo and the further price rise, 1973-74
notes.b: Alongside the price rise the Arab producers cut off supplies to particular countries. The price rise, however, affected every importer, and it did not end when the embargo did.
points: An embargo (a ban on supplying a country) was imposed on the USA from 19-20 October 1973 and on the Netherlands from 21 October, as supporters of Israel.
The Netherlands was targeted because its government was pro-Israel and because Rotterdam was Europe's main oil port, so an embargo there threatened supplies across the continent.
The posted price was raised again in December 1973. By early 1974 oil cost about four times its pre-war price, in other words prices roughly quadrupled.
The embargo was lifted in March 1974, but prices stayed high. Only the USA and the Netherlands were embargoed, whereas every oil-importing country faced the price rise.
notes.tip: Keep the embargo (stopping supply to named countries) separate from the price rise (felt by all importers). Examiners ask what the embargo was, who was targeted and one effect.

notes.h: Immediate effects: fuel saving and the three-day week
notes.b: Governments' first response to scarce, expensive oil was to cut the amount of fuel people used. The winter of 1973-74 brought visible disruption to daily life.
points: Car-free Sundays were introduced in the Netherlands and West Germany in the winter of 1973-74, so that people used less petrol.
Speed limits were reduced and households were asked to turn down their heating, which saved fuel at little cost.
The Netherlands also issued ration coupons for petrol, which is fuel rationing (limiting each person's share), because it had been embargoed.

Britain introduced a three-day working week for industry from January to March 1974 under Edward Heath's government. A miners' overtime ban and dispute added to the electricity shortage, so industry could use power on only three days.
notes.tip: When you describe rationing, name the Netherlands. Do not say that Britain rationed petrol: its emergency measure was the three-day week.

notes.h: Economic effects: inflation, deficits and stagflation
notes.b: The shock raised costs everywhere at once. The result was a new and awkward combination of problems that the policies of the boom years could not solve.
points: Oil-importing states had to pay far more for their imports, so they ran balance-of-payments deficits (spending more abroad than they earned).
The Arab producers gained huge revenues called petrodollars, which were recycled through Western banks.
Industrial production fell, and unemployment rose from the low levels of the 1960s, with the sharpest increases in heavy industry, which used a great deal of energy.
Inflation rose sharply while output stagnated. This combination is called stagflation (stagnation plus inflation), which is different from an ordinary recession or from inflation alone.
Keynesian remedies struggled because they treat one problem at a time: boosting demand to cut unemployment pushed prices higher, while cutting demand to curb inflation made unemployment worse.
Fighting inflation replaced full employment as the priority of Thatcher's government, which is why monetarism (explained later) replaced Keynesian demand management in Britain.
notes.tip: Strong essays on the oil crisis list causes and trigger, immediate effects (price, embargo, rationing, inflation) and longer-term effects, so keep these effects separate from the immediate fuel-saving measures.

notes.h: The second oil shock, recession and unemployment, 1979-1990
notes.b: A second shock in 1979 pushed economies back into recession, and unemployment became the defining problem of the early 1980s.
points: The Iranian revolution of 1979 caused a second oil shock. Prices roughly doubled between 1978 and 1980, and Western economies fell into recession in 1980-82.
Unemployment across the EEC rose from low levels in the early 1970s to above 10 per cent by the mid-1980s, with Spain and Ireland suffering much higher rates.
British unemployment reached about three million in 1982. It was worst in heavy industry and in the north of England, Scotland and Wales, where factories, mines and yards closed.
Riots in English cities in 1981, including Brixton and Toxteth, showed the social strain of unemployment.
Mass unemployment also strained the welfare state, because more people claimed benefits while fewer paid taxes.
notes.tip: Do not confuse the first oil shock (1973-74, Yom Kippur War) with the second (1979, Iranian revolution). Cause-and-result questions ask why unemployment rose after 1979.

notes.b: Higher energy costs and foreign competition left older industries unable to survive. Governments also looked for ways to rely less on imported oil.
points: Deindustrialisation means the decline of manufacturing and heavy industry in an economy. In Britain steel, coal and shipbuilding declined sharply, changing the regional economies of the north and Scotland.
The EEC introduced steel quotas in 1980, known as the Davignon Plan after Etienne Davignon, the commissioner for industry, to limit output as older industries were cut back across Europe.
West Germany's industry moved up-market into machinery and cars, so it adapted better than Britain, which relied on older industries.

France announced a nuclear power programme in 1974, the Messmer Plan (after Prime Minister Pierre Messmer). By the late 1980s nuclear power gave about 70 per cent of French electricity, cutting oil dependence.
North Sea oil began to flow in the mid-1970s. By about 1980 Britain was self-sufficient in oil and Norway a major exporter, which cushioned both against the second shock.
The International Energy Agency was set up in 1974 under the OECD to coordinate oil stocks and policy among importing states. Energy conservation and coal were also promoted.
notes.tip: Examiners ask about the response of governments, so name the policy and the country: the Messmer Plan for France, North Sea oil for Britain and Norway, and the Davignon Plan for steel.

notes.h: Significance of the Oil Crisis and differing views
notes.b: The oil crisis marked a turning point in Western politics and economics, but historians disagree about how much of the change it actually caused.
points: The crisis ended the long boom and exposed the dependence of Western prosperity on cheap energy. Political attention shifted from growth to inflation and unemployment.
It strengthened the case for the EEC to act together, leading to the European Monetary System in 1979. There is more on this in the notes on European unity.

Contemporaries blamed the Arab embargo and OPEC. Many economists later argued that inflation, the end of Bretton Woods and falling productivity were already weakening the boom, so the oil shock hastened the end rather than causing it alone.

The embargo gave oil-producing states a new role in world politics. Western states looked for energy independence through nuclear power, North Sea oil and conservation, but unemployment and industrial decline remained.
notes.tip: Examiners ask how lasting the impact was. Do not say flatly that the oil crisis caused the end of the boom; separate the shock from the other causes.

notes.b: Thatcher was Prime Minister from 1979 to 1990 and the dominant figure in Britain's response to the post-1973 economy. Her rise was shaped by the failure of the government before her.
points: She was born in Grantham on 13 October 1925, the daughter of a grocer, Alfred Roberts. She studied chemistry at Somerville College, Oxford, was called to the bar in 1953 and became MP for Finchley in 1959.
She was Secretary of State for Education and Science in Edward Heath's government from 1970 to 1974.

Heath lost both general elections of 1974, in February and October, which damaged his authority. Keith Joseph, who shaped monetarist ideas, founded the Centre for Policy Studies with Thatcher in 1974.
She was elected Conservative leader on 11 February 1975. Heath was knocked out in the first ballot and she then won the second ballot against Willie Whitelaw.
She became Prime Minister on 4 May 1979, defeating James Callaghan's Labour government after the winter of discontent of 1978-79.

As leader she was a participant, not a combatant, in every episode that follows. She was shaped by Heath's failure, the crisis of the 1970s and Joseph's ideas, and she in turn shaped events as Prime Minister.
notes.tip: When explaining her rise, mention both 1974 elections, and do not say simply that she defeated Heath: it took two ballots.

notes.h: Key personality: Margaret Thatcher, monetarism and economic policy
notes.b: Thatcher believed that inflation, not unemployment, was the main problem. Her government set out to cut it by controlling the money supply, even at a high cost.
points: Monetarism is the belief that inflation is controlled by limiting the money supply (the amount of money in circulation). It was associated with Milton Friedman, and it differs from Keynesianism, which manages demand.
Chancellor Geoffrey Howe introduced the Medium Term Financial Strategy in 1980, setting targets for the money supply and government borrowing.
Howe's 1981 budget raised taxes during a recession, so 364 economists signed a letter of protest.
Inflation fell from double figures in 1980 (about 18 per cent) to under 5 per cent by 1983. Unemployment passed three million in 1982.
Public spending growth was cut, but the core of the welfare state, such as health care and pensions, was not dismantled.
notes.tip: Essays on Thatcher need a date and a named policy for each point, so give the Medium Term Financial Strategy (1980) and the 1981 budget, not just monetarism.

notes.h: Key personality: Margaret Thatcher, privatisation and trade union laws
notes.b: Thatcher wanted to extend capitalism by selling state assets and by reducing the power of the trade unions. Both policies changed the balance between the state and the market.
points: Privatisation is the sale of state-owned firms to private shareholders. British Telecom was privatised in 1984, British Gas in 1986 and British Airways in 1987.
The Housing Act of 1980 gave council tenants the right to buy their homes. Exchange controls (limits on moving money abroad) were abolished in October 1979.
Deregulation, which means removing rules rather than selling firms, came in the City in October 1986, known as the Big Bang.
The Employment Act 1980 limited secondary picketing and restricted the closed shop (a workplace where all workers must join the union).
The Employment Act 1982 further limited the closed shop and made unions liable for damages, so they risked financial loss from unlawful strikes.
The Trade Union Act 1984 required secret ballots for strikes and for union executives. Together the acts reduced the power of the unions step by step.
notes.tip: Do not confuse privatisation (selling state firms) with deregulation (removing rules, as in the City in 1986). Know all three union laws with their years.

notes.h: Key personality: Margaret Thatcher, the Falklands War and elections
notes.b: The Falklands War rescued her popularity at a time of high unemployment. It helped lead to a landslide in 1983 and the longest unbroken term of the century.
points: Argentina invaded the Falkland Islands on 2 April 1982. Thatcher, as Prime Minister, sent a task force, although she was not herself a combatant.
Argentine forces surrendered on 14 June 1982. Her popularity recovered and she won a landslide in June 1983.
She won the general elections of 1979, 1983 and 1987. At about eleven and a half years she had the longest continuous term of any Prime Minister in the twentieth century.
notes.tip: Say that Thatcher sent the task force. Do not describe her as a participant in the fighting.

notes.b: The strike was the most severe test of Thatcher's trade union policy and the biggest industrial confrontation of her premiership.
points: The strike began in March 1984, after the closure of Cortonwood pit was announced and National Coal Board chairman Ian MacGregor announced a closure programme.
Arthur Scargill, leader of the National Union of Mineworkers, called the strike without holding a national ballot, which divided the miners and weakened their case.
The government had built up coal stocks beforehand, so power stations could keep running, and it used mass policing. Violent clashes occurred at Orgreave on 18 June 1984.
The miners returned to work in March 1985 without a settlement. The defeat weakened the unions and speeded the closure of pits.
notes.tip: Cause-and-result questions ask why the miners lost. Give the lack of a ballot, the coal stocks and the policing. Do not confuse Orgreave (the June 1984 clash) with Cortonwood (the pit whose threatened closure started the strike).

notes.h: Thatcher, Europe, the USA and the USSR
notes.b: Abroad, she combined a close partnership with the USA, hard bargaining within the EEC and a willingness to talk to the Soviet Union.
points: Her relationship with President Ronald Reagan was close. US cruise missiles were deployed at Greenham Common from 1983, and in April 1986 US aircraft flew from British bases in the raid on Libya.
A Soviet newspaper nicknamed her the "Iron Lady" in January 1976, a name she later adopted with some pride.
She met Mikhail Gorbachev at Chequers in December 1984 and said he was a man she could "do business with". She then helped to persuade Reagan that he was sincere.
At the Fontainebleau European Council in June 1984 she won the British budget rebate, reducing Britain's net contribution to the EEC budget.
She supported the Single European Act of 1986 because it created the single market, but she opposed economic and monetary union and the Social Charter.
In her Bruges speech of 20 September 1988 she argued against a federal Europe, while still supporting the single market. Britain joined the Exchange Rate Mechanism in October 1990.
She signed the Anglo-Irish Agreement with Taoiseach Garret FitzGerald on 15 November 1985 at Hillsborough, giving the Irish government a consultative role in Northern Ireland.
notes.tip: In essays on attitudes to Europe, state her position explicitly: she was a supporter of the single market and an opponent of federalism, with Fontainebleau, the Single European Act and Bruges as evidence. Do not mix up Fontainebleau (1984, rebate) with Bruges (1988, speech). There is more on this in the notes on European unity.

notes.h: Key personality: Margaret Thatcher, her fall in 1990
notes.b: Thatcher's fall came from within her own party, over Europe and over the poll tax, even though she had won three elections.
points: The poll tax (Community Charge) was introduced in Scotland in 1989 and in England and Wales in 1990. It was deeply unpopular because everyone paid the same charge.
Geoffrey Howe resigned on 1 November 1990 over her European policy and made a critical speech on 13 November.
Michael Heseltine then challenged her for the leadership. She won the first ballot on 20 November 1990 but not by the margin required.
She announced her resignation on 22 November 1990 and left office on 28 November, when John Major succeeded her.
notes.tip: Say that she announced her resignation on 22 November and left office on 28 November. Examiners ask why Thatcher fell, so give Howe, Heseltine, Europe and the poll tax.

notes.h: Key personality: Margaret Thatcher, how she was seen
notes.b: Few modern politicians divide opinion as sharply as Thatcher. Contemporaries and historians weigh her record differently.
points: Contemporary supporters admired her resolve and credited her with ending Britain's economic decline.
Contemporary critics pointed to unemployment passing three million in 1982, deindustrialisation, social division, the gap between north and south, and the poll tax.

Historians debate whether her policies were a decisive break with the post-war settlement or the continuation of trends already under way, such as the oil shock, the decline of heavy industry and the rise of finance.
Thatcherism, the name given to her free-market approach, has remained a lasting legacy in later politics.
notes.tip: Name "supporters" and "critics" rather than individual historians, and give your own judgement.

notes.h: Assessment: successes and failures of the 1970s and 1980s
notes.b: The record of the Western economies after 1973 is judged on whether they restored growth and whether the costs of adjustment were fair. Thatcher is the best test case.
points: Achievements: inflation was reduced, trade union power was curbed, privatisation made a more flexible economy, and Britain's profile in Europe and with the USA was raised.
Limits: mass unemployment, the decline of manufacturing and mining communities, regional inequality, the poll tax and her fall in 1990.
Supporters of Thatcher regard her as having reversed Britain's relative decline, while critics regard the decline of manufacturing as a heavy and lasting cost.
The oil shock hastened rather than solely caused the end of the boom, since inflation and industrial change were already under way.
How lasting was its impact? Energy policy changed, but unemployment and industrial decline remained.
Contemporaries blamed OPEC and the embargo, whereas later historians stress the weaknesses already present in the economy.
notes.tip: The Higher essay on Thatcher rewards a stated judgement that balances achievements (inflation, union reform, privatisation, the Falklands, the rebate) against costs (unemployment, industrial decline, social division, the poll tax, her fall in 1990).

keyTerms.definition: An economic system in which private owners run businesses for profit in competitive markets, which Thatcher's government sought to strengthen.
A system in which the state provides health care, pensions, unemployment benefit and education to citizens, funded mainly through taxation and insurance.
A combination of stagnant output, high unemployment and rising prices, which challenged conventional economic policy in the 1970s.
The economic doctrine that controlling the money supply is the key to controlling inflation, which Thatcher's government adopted.
The sale of state-owned companies to private owners, such as British Telecom in 1984.
The decline of manufacturing and heavy industry as a share of an economy's output and employment.
The Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries, formed in 1960, whose members set oil prices and output; its price rises of 1973 and 1979 caused the oil shocks.
A sudden and large rise in the price of oil, as in 1973–74 and 1979, which raised costs and inflation in importing countries.
Thatcher's Employment Acts of 1980 and 1982 and Trade Union Act of 1984, which restricted secondary picketing and the closed shop and required ballots.
